newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany mulls tougher laws against sex offenders.
newsitem.headline: Germany mulls tougher laws against sex offenders.

text.p: A German political leader said on Sunday a central registry used to hunt Nazi war criminals could become a model for a new system to track down and prosecute sexual criminals.

"This model has proved its worth in the past with the investigation of Nazi crimes," Rita Suessmuth, president of the German parliament, wrote in Bild am Sonntag newspaper. "This is the only way we will be able to shed light on this horribly dark chapter."

Thousands of Nazi criminals were brought to justice after World War Two with the aid of a central investigation agency in Ludwigsburg, which assisted local prosecutors in collecting evidence and preparing charges.

Suessmuth's proposal came just hours after 14-year-old Sabine Wojdylo was found dead in a swamp near her school in the northwestern town of Leverkusen after being sexually abused and bludgeoned to death, police said on Sunday.

"We have found evidence at the scene of the crime and from the autopsy that a sexual offence was committed," said detective Manfred Pennartz, head of the homicide commission. "The cause of death was a bludgeoning to her neck."

Authorities said they were searching for a man aged about 30 seen following the girl shortly before she disappeared. They said the suspect matches the description of a man sought for four rapes this year in Leverkusen.
The attack was the latest in a series of crimes on children to haunt Germany and other parts of Europe.
Germans were horrified in September by the brutal rape and murder of a seven-year-old Bavarian schoolgirl by a convicted sex criminal who had recently been released from detention.
The murder of seven-year-old Natalie Astner prompted calls for chemical castration of paedophiles, stiffer sentencing and an end to early releases for sex offenders.

The mix of outrage and frustration in Germany in the wake of Natalie's death mirrored the mood in neighbouring Belgium, where investigators have uncovered a child porn ring alleged to have been run by a sex offender also released early from prison.

Last week hundreds of police searched in vain for a seven-year-old Cologne girl who disappeared from a playground. She was found 30 hours later when a 31-year-old man handed her over to a streetcar driver, who was later arrested on suspicion of sexual abuse.
With intense media coverage of sexual crimes, the Bonn government has been moving to tighten controls.
Justice Minister Edzard Schmidt-Jortzig said in a radio interview on Sunday the federal government was planning to clamp down on states that failed adequately to punish sex offenders.
"Federal laws may have to make some things obligatory that the states already have the power to do now but do not do effectively enough," Schmidt-Joertzig told SDR radio.
The minister, who has been holding hearings on sexual crimes in Bonn, said the coalition government would be discussing ways to tighten laws against sexual crimes this week.
Suessmuth said it was unacceptable that sexual offenders were being released from detention because of legal loopholes and insufficient coordination between various agencies.
"Federal and state lawmakers need to close these loopholes immediately," she said. "There is an urgent need to speed up investigations and prosecutions and to improve the methods of prisoner review."
